issues.description: The UML in the problem statement defines Animal with two attributes (name: String and age: int) and a constructor Animal(String, int) (problem_statement.md, UML lines). The reference solution's Animal class provides only a single String name attribute and a constructor Animal(String) (solution_repository/src/de/tum/cit/ase/Animal.java: lines 3-8). This mismatch (constructor parameters and the presence/absence of the age attribute) will confuse students about which constructor and attributes they must implement and may cause tests or instructor-provided code to disagree with student implementations.
issues.suggested_fix: Make the constructor/attribute requirements consistent across artifacts. Either (A) update the UML and any references in the problem statement to remove the age attribute and specify a single-argument constructor Animal(String) (so students implement only name, matching the solution), or (B) update the solution (and tests) to include the age attribute and a two-argument constructor Animal(String, int) with accompanying getter/setter for age. Option A is recommended because the textual description emphasizes only the name and the provided solution and example usage use a single-argument constructor.

issues.description: There is an internal contradiction within the problem statement: the narrative/text explicitly states that "All three animals have something in common: they have a name" (implying name is the common attribute), while the UML diagram for Animal includes an age attribute (age: int) and a two-argument constructor. This conflicting guidance may lead students to wonder whether age must be implemented and whether constructors should accept age.
issues.suggested_fix: Clarify the problem statement so text and UML agree. Either mention in the text that animals have both name and age and show the corresponding constructor and accessors in examples, or remove the age attribute from the UML so the text (and the rest of the exercise) consistently treat name as the only required common attribute.
